standard_prerequisites.name: Induced transformation
standard_prerequisites.statement: The induced transformation on a subinterval is defined by the first return time of its points to the subinterval.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the transformation about which the statement is made.

standard_prerequisites.name: Conjugacy equation
standard_prerequisites.statement: For a symmetric transformation the reflection of the whole interval conjugates it to its inverse off the discontinuities.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the equation the induced transformation is asserted to satisfy.

standard_prerequisites.name: Symmetry of subintervals
standard_prerequisites.statement: A subinterval is either alpha-symmetric for a continuity interval or symmetric about the middle of the whole interval.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the case distinction along which the proof runs.

core_obligations: For an alpha-symmetric subinterval, take a point that is not a discontinuity of the induced transformation and express the induced image as a high iterate of the point (source line 631).

Rewrite the conjugate of that image by the conjugacy equation, so that the problem becomes the comparison of the inverse induced transformation with the inverse iterate applied to the conjugate of the point (source lines 633-637).
Justify the comparison with the local reflection lemma, which says that an iterate of the point stays in the subinterval exactly when its conjugate does, and conclude (source line 639).
Repeat the argument in the case of a subinterval symmetric about the middle of the whole interval, where the reflection of the induced point is handled directly (source lines 641-645).

proof_roadmap.step: Reduce the equation for the induced transformation to a comparison of two inverse iterates.
Use the local reflection lemma to justify the comparison.
Treat the subinterval symmetric about the middle of the whole interval separately.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 626-628: the transformation induced by a symmetric interval exchange transformation on a symmetric subinterval again satisfies the conjugacy equation between the reflection and the inverse. The proof (source lines 630-646) has to relate the return time to the subinterval with the return time to itself along the orbit, and the identification of the two inverse iterates is justified not by computation but by the local reflection lemma, which says that an iterate of a point lies in the subinterval exactly when its conjugate does; a second case, where the subinterval is symmetric about the middle of the whole interval rather than about a continuity interval, is then treated separately. The statement records the conjugacy equation and neither the return-time comparison nor the case distinction.
